_about: PRO rewrite pass 3: era-1 scenes 79-117 in play order.

scenarios.title: The First Fine
scenarios.text: A fine slip in your locker after the first team flight: a dress-code violation you didn't know existed. Your socks, apparently, were the wrong color, and the veterans have already framed a photo of them.

choices.label: Laugh and pay it
choices.result: Paid in cash, with a grin, and you wear the loudest socks you own to the next team meal. The room loves it, and the fine committee adds a new rule in your honor.

choices.label: Read the whole rulebook
choices.result: The full team rulebook, forty pages, read in bed that night. You find two more rules you've been breaking and fix both before anyone notices.

choices.label: Pay it and go kick
choices.result: Paid, with some grumbling, and the irritation goes straight into an extra session at the net. Your leg feels better than your pride by dinner.

scenarios.title: The Meal Money
scenarios.text: The per diem envelope on the first road trip is thicker than any scholarship check you ever got in college. The veterans are already planning where theirs is going tonight.

choices.label: Put it in the bank
choices.result: The whole envelope goes in the bank, and you eat the team meals. By December the road trips have quietly paid for your offseason trainer.

choices.label: Take the rookies out
choices.result: The rookie class eats like kings for one night on your envelope. It's gone by dessert, and four rookies will remember it for years.

choices.label: Treat yourself, a little
choices.result: A good dinner alone, a good book from the airport and a long nap. It feels like being a grown-up, and you send {parent} a photo of the dessert.

scenarios.title: Rookie Year Taxes
scenarios.text: Your first tax bill as a pro arrives in a thick envelope: a number nobody prepared you for, due in a month, with forms from every state you played a road game in.

choices.label: Hire an athletes' accountant
choices.result: An accountant who only works with athletes takes the whole envelope off your hands. It's done in two weeks, correctly, and you learn what a 'jock tax' is.

choices.label: Ask a veteran at lunch
choices.result: One veteran at lunch gives you his accountant's number and a story about his first year that makes you laugh until your stomach hurts.

choices.label: Do it yourself
choices.result: A long weekend with spreadsheets and coffee. It's stressful, probably right, and you feel strangely proud when you click the last button.

scenarios.title: Free Cleats
scenarios.text: A shoe company offers you free cleats and a small contract, if you wear them on camera. The cleats are bright orange, and your old pair has been with you since college.

choices.label: Sign and lace up
choices.result: Signed, and the orange cleats arrive the next day. They're fine, the check pays for your offseason training, and the veterans call you 'traffic cone'.

choices.label: Test them for a week
choices.result: A week of testing before you sign anything. They're good, so you sign, with a clause that lets you wear your old pair if they ever hurt.

choices.label: Keep your old cleats
choices.result: Your old cleats stay. Your feet are happy and your account is the same, and the equipment manager pats them like an old dog.

scenarios.title: The Kicking Ball Room
scenarios.text: The equipment staff prepares the game balls in a back room that smells like leather and brushes, and you have opinions about how the balls feel. Nobody has asked for them yet.

choices.label: Learn how it's done
choices.result: An afternoon in the ball room with the staff, watching every step. Your opinions get much better informed, and much quieter.

choices.label: Thank the staff every day
choices.result: A thank-you after every practice, every day. By October they start showing you the game balls on Friday, which nobody else gets.

choices.label: Kick every practice ball
choices.result: Every practice ball, kicked, until you can feel the difference between them in your sleep. Your leg aches, and the balls stop surprising you.

scenarios.title: The Trainer's Table
scenarios.text: The athletic trainer presses a thumb into your hip and says your hip flexor is tight. You think it's nothing. The trainer is still pressing, and looking at you over their glasses.

choices.label: Do the stretches
choices.result: Every stretch, every day, exactly as written. The tightness is gone in a week, and the trainer says 'told you' with great satisfaction.

choices.label: Kick on it anyway
choices.result: Kicking through it works: the hip holds. It nags all month, like a stone in your shoe, and you start every practice a little worried.

choices.label: Take a day off kicking
choices.result: A full day off kicking, which feels like a crime. It helps more than you'd like to admit, and you come back loose.

scenarios.title: Your First Locker
scenarios.text: Your name is on a strip of tape above a locker between two veterans who haven't introduced themselves. One is eating a sandwich. The other is staring at you like you're a rumor.

choices.label: Introduce yourself to both
choices.result: A handshake from one, a grunt from the other. By October, the grunt is your favorite person in the building and steals your snacks.

choices.label: Let your work introduce you
choices.result: Head down, work loud. It takes a month, and when the welcome comes it's real: the grunting veteran saves you a seat on the plane.

choices.label: Make the locker yours
choices.result: A photo of your family and a paper calendar go up first. It makes the place feel like yours, and {parent} asks for a picture of it.

scenarios.title: The Group Text
scenarios.text: The specialists have a group text, you've learned. It's very active, it's apparently hilarious, it has a name nobody will tell you, and you're not in it yet.

choices.label: Ask the punter to add you
choices.result: In by lunch, at your own request. The first message after you join is a meme about your haircut, which is how you know you're in.

choices.label: Wait to be added
choices.result: No asking. After a good week of practice, you're added without a word, and {holder} sends a single thumbs-up that feels like a medal.

choices.label: Live without it
choices.result: No group text, no notifications. It's quieter, and you miss every inside joke in the specialists' room for a month.

scenarios.title: The Ride to Practice
scenarios.text: You don't have a car yet, and the veteran who offered you rides keeps forgetting. You've been standing in the parking lot of your building at six in the morning twice this week.

choices.label: Ride with another rookie
choices.result: Rides with {backup}, every day. The drives turn into the best part of the week: bad music, worse coffee, and the start of a real friendship.

choices.label: Take a car service
choices.result: A car service, a book and twenty quiet minutes. It's expensive and relaxing, and you arrive calmer than anyone in the building.

choices.label: Bike to practice
choices.result: Five miles each way on a secondhand bike. Your legs are tired by Wednesday and strong by October, and the strength coach loves it.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Show
scenarios.text: The rookies have to put on a talent show for the veterans on the last night of camp. Your only talent is kicking, and the stage is a cafeteria table.

choices.label: Read a poem about the snapper
choices.result: A dramatic poetry reading about the long snapper's hands, with a candle. The room cries laughing, and the snapper asks for a copy.

choices.label: Run the whole show
choices.result: The rookies' acts, organized and timed like a practice script. It's the best show in years, and {coach} asks who ran it.

choices.label: Do a card trick
choices.result: One card trick, and you sit down. It's fine, nobody remembers it by breakfast, and you sleep well while the veterans argue about the poem.

scenarios.title: The Fan Event
scenarios.text: At a season-ticket holders' event in a hotel ballroom, everyone wants a picture with the new kicker. An old man in a thirty-year-old jersey is first in line.

choices.label: Take every picture
choices.result: Every picture, and a dozen names learned. The old man and his wife sit behind the bench for years after, waving at you before every game.

choices.label: Bring the specialists along
choices.result: The punter, the snapper and {holder} join you, and the fans love the 'kicking unit' photo. It ends up on the team's website.

choices.label: Stay your hour
choices.result: Your hour, then home to the couch. It's perfectly fine, you don't learn a single name, and the old man in the jersey waves at somebody else.

scenarios.title: The Hometown Paper
scenarios.text: Your hometown paper runs a full-page story about you, with a photo from your senior prom: the rented suit, the haircut, the corsage. The veterans have already found it.

choices.label: Send them a better photo
choices.result: A call to the paper, a laugh, and a better photo sent over. They run both side by side the next week, and {parent} buys ten copies.

choices.label: Own the prom photo
choices.result: The prom photo stays. By Friday it's taped to your locker, courtesy of the veterans, and you sign it for them.

choices.label: Thank the reporter
choices.result: A thank-you call to the reporter who wrote it. They become the first person to tell your story right, and they'll be at your retirement.

scenarios.title: The Card Signing
scenarios.text: A trading card company wants your signature on a thousand cards in one afternoon, in a hotel conference room with bad coffee and a man counting.

choices.label: Sign all thousand
choices.result: A thousand signatures in four hours. Your hand hurts for two days, the check is nice, and your signature gets worse with every hundred.

choices.label: Sign some for charity
choices.result: Two hundred cards, and a full set donated to a children's hospital raffle. The raffle raises more than the check would have.

choices.label: Pass on the cards
choices.result: No cards this time. Your hand is grateful, and the company signs a punter instead, who sends you a smug photo of his check.

scenarios.title: The Holder Who Won't Talk
scenarios.text: Your new holder is all business and doesn't talk to rookies: no small talk, no jokes, just the laces and the spot. Three practices in, you've heard eleven words.

choices.label: Learn the routine by watching
choices.result: No words needed: you learn {holder}'s routine by watching every rep. By week three, you're in sync without a word, and that's its own kind of friendship.

choices.label: Win the holder over
choices.result: Lunch, questions about their family, patience. It takes a month, and then {holder} won't stop talking, mostly about their dog.

choices.label: Out-prepare the holder
choices.result: Early every day, until {holder} starts showing up even earlier. Neither of you says a word about it, and the holds get very clean.

scenarios.title: The First Night Game
scenarios.text: Your first night game under the stadium lights is tomorrow, and you can't sleep. It's two in the morning, and the hotel air conditioner sounds like a crowd.

choices.label: Do nothing all day
choices.result: Reading, a long nap and absolutely nothing else all day. You're calm by warmups, which surprises everyone, including you, and the snapper asks your secret.

choices.label: Call the team psychologist
choices.result: The team psychologist answers at seven and gives you two breathing exercises. You use both, and the lights feel smaller.

choices.label: Call {parent}
choices.result: {parent} tells you about every night game he ever watched you play, back to peewee. You laugh yourself to sleep by three.

scenarios.title: Sleeping on the Plane
scenarios.text: The team plane leaves at midnight, and you have never once slept on a plane. The veterans have pillows shaped like footballs and a card game going in the back.

choices.label: Bring a sleep kit
choices.result: An eye mask, earplugs and a pillow. The veterans mock you mercilessly, and you sleep four hours while they don't.

choices.label: Join the card game
choices.result: The card game in the back, for matchsticks, not money. You lose badly and make three friends who teach you every rule wrong.

choices.label: Watch film all flight
choices.result: Film on your tablet the whole flight. You land exhausted and very prepared, and {coach} sees the screen on the way off the plane.

scenarios.title: The Hotel Roommate
scenarios.text: Your road roommate snores, sleepwalks and talks about his ex all night. Last trip he tried to leave the room in his sleep, and you caught him at the elevator.

choices.label: Listen to him
choices.result: Listening, mostly. He's going through a lot, and you become his person on road trips, the one he calls after the bad weeks.

choices.label: Ask for a new roommate
choices.result: The travel staff finds you a new roommate. You sleep, and he's a little hurt, and lunch is awkward for a week.

choices.label: Earplugs and house rules
choices.result: Earplugs, a lights-out time and a chair against the door. It mostly works, and he starts calling you 'the warden'.

scenarios.title: The Waiver Wire
scenarios.text: A rookie from your class is cut on Tuesday morning and claimed by another club within an hour. His locker is empty before you've finished your coffee.

choices.label: Text him congratulations
choices.result: A congratulations text, sent before lunch. He calls every Sunday that season to compare notes on being new, and you end up rooting for his team twice.

choices.label: Treat it as a lesson
choices.result: A lesson about how fast this league moves, written on the inside of your locker door. You kick extra that afternoon.

choices.label: Feel it, then sleep
choices.result: One evening to feel it: the speed, the empty locker, the coffee going cold. Then you go to sleep, and the next day is just a day.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Contract
scenarios.text: You finally read your rookie contract all the way through, at the kitchen table, with a highlighter. It's forty pages, and some of the words you've only seen in movies.

choices.label: Call your agent with questions
choices.result: Six questions to your agent, by phone, for an hour. You learn what a guarantee really means and which clause could cut you for nothing.

choices.label: Tape up the incentives
choices.result: The incentive clauses go inside your locker door, highlighted in yellow. Every practice has a number attached to it now, and you can't stop seeing them.

choices.label: Trust your agent
choices.result: Skimmed, and trusted to your agent. It's fine, probably, the highlighter dries out in the drawer, and you never quite learn what's in there.

scenarios.title: The Kicker Down the Hall
scenarios.text: The punter is your age and acts like he's been in the league twenty years: tells you where to stand, how to stretch, which coffee to drink. You share a meeting room every day.

choices.label: Become friends anyway
choices.result: Friends, anyway, over a month of bad coffee. It turns out he's as nervous as you are and has been faking it since camp.

choices.label: Make every drill a contest
choices.result: Every specialist drill becomes a quiet competition between you. You both get better, and the coaches start scheduling you together.

choices.label: Keep your distance
choices.result: Polite distance. The specialists' room is awkward all season, and you notice how quiet it is when he's not there.

scenarios.title: The Film You Hate
scenarios.text: The coaches pull up your college film in a dark meeting room, and it looks completely different from how you remembered it: slower, stiffer, younger. Someone pauses on your worst kick.

choices.label: Write down every flaw
choices.result: Every flaw the coaches point out goes on a list. It's a long list, two pages, and you laminate it and keep it in your kicking bag all season.

choices.label: Fix one thing a week
choices.result: One flaw a week, fixed and charted. By midseason, the old film looks like someone else's, and {coach} uses it to teach the rookies.

choices.label: Call your college coach
choices.result: Your college coach watches the same film that night and calls back laughing: he always knew about the plant foot. You talk for an hour.

scenarios.title: Your Parents in the Stands
scenarios.text: {parent} drives eleven hours to see you kick in person for the first time as a pro. He arrives a day early, in his old team jacket, with a cooler of sandwiches.

choices.label: Spend every minute together
choices.result: Every free minute, together: the hotel breakfast, the walk around the stadium, the sandwiches. He doesn't stop smiling all weekend.

choices.label: Give him the full tour
choices.result: The full tour: the locker room, the field, the coaches. He shakes {coach}'s hand twice and tells the equipment manager about your peewee days.

choices.label: Stick to game-week habits
choices.result: Your routine stays exactly the same, and you see him after. He understands completely, and you wish, driving home, that you'd done more.

scenarios.title: The Sibling Who Wants to Visit
scenarios.text: {sibling} wants to spend spring break at your apartment: a week of sleeping on your couch, eating your food and seeing what the league is like up close.

choices.label: Take him everywhere
choices.result: Everywhere, all week: practice, the team cafeteria, the stadium at night. {sibling} thinks you're the coolest person alive, and says so to everyone.

choices.label: Put him to work
choices.result: Your youth clinic gets a volunteer for a week, and {sibling} turns out to be great with the kids. You see him differently after it.

choices.label: Say not this year
choices.result: Not this spring, you explain; it's too busy. {sibling} is disappointed, goes to a friend's beach house instead, and sends you a photo of the ocean.

scenarios.title: The College Teammates' Chat
scenarios.text: Your old college teammates' group chat is on fire: everyone wants inside stories from the league. Who's mean, who's rich, who's actually funny. They're asking you by name.

choices.label: Tell the funny ones
choices.result: The funny stories, yes; the private ones, never. The chat loves you, and {best_friend} starts calling you 'the insider' in every single message.

choices.label: Keep the team private
choices.result: The team stays private, you explain. It's a little awkward, and it's right, and two old teammates respect it more than they say.

choices.label: Mute the chat
choices.result: Muted for the season. You miss some good jokes, and come back in January to four thousand messages and a nickname you'll never shake.

scenarios.title: The Old Flame
scenarios.text: Someone you dated in college messages you the week your first big headline runs. It's friendly, a little nostalgic, and it's the first time you've heard from them in two years.

choices.label: Meet for coffee
choices.result: Coffee, an hour that turns into three. It's warm and a little strange, you're glad you went, and you both leave it there.

choices.label: Ask yourself why now
choices.result: Why now? You don't answer it, even to yourself, and keep things friendly from a distance. The messages fade by the end of the month.

choices.label: Leave it on read
choices.result: Left on read. It's simpler, and on bad nights you wonder about it for a minute before you fall asleep.

scenarios.title: Your First Bad Practice Week
scenarios.text: Five bad practices in a row, and the coaches have stopped saying 'next one'. On the sixth day, nobody says anything at all, which is worse.

choices.label: Strip it back with {coach}
choices.result: {coach} strips your routine back to the basics: three steps, one thought, no extras. It's humbling to start over, and by Thursday it works.

choices.label: Kick until it's back
choices.result: Every night, until the field lights come on, until it's back. Your leg is heavy, and the sixth bad practice never comes.

choices.label: Talk it through with {holder}
choices.result: {holder} has seen this before and says so over coffee: everybody hits the wall once. It helps more than the kicking.

scenarios.title: The Veteran's Car
scenarios.text: A veteran tosses you his keys after practice and asks you to move his car. It costs more than your parents' house, it's parked on a slope, and it's raining.

choices.label: Move it very carefully
choices.result: Very, very carefully. He notices how carefully, and from then on he calls you by your name instead of 'kicker'.

choices.label: Ask what it cost him
choices.result: What did it cost, and would he do it again? His answer is long and honest, and it's about much more than the car.

choices.label: Hand the keys back
choices.result: Not comfortable driving it, you admit. He laughs, moves it himself in the rain and tells the story at lunch, kindly, with you as the sensible one.

scenarios.title: Learning to Cook
scenarios.text: Your first apartment, and your diet is cereal, takeout and whatever the team cafeteria sends home with you. The nutritionist has started looking at you sadly.

choices.label: Learn five meals
choices.result: Five meals, learned and cooked on rotation. Your energy in practice is better within a week, and you can make a very good omelet.

choices.label: Start a cooking night
choices.result: A Sunday cooking night with two rookies and {backup}. Everyone burns something, the fire alarm goes off twice, and nobody cares in the slightest.

choices.label: Sign up for a meal service
choices.result: A meal service, expensive and perfect. You never think about food again, never learn to cook, and the delivery driver knows your schedule better than you.

scenarios.title: The Team Nutritionist
scenarios.text: The team nutritionist reviews three days of what you've eaten, one page at a time, and doesn't hide her reaction to the gas station burritos.

choices.label: Follow her plan
choices.result: Her plan, to the letter. You feel better by week two, and she puts a gold star on your locker, which you pretend to hate.

choices.label: Ask for a kicking plan
choices.result: A plan built for kicking power, strict and specific. It's hard to follow and it works, and your leg feels heavier in a good way.

choices.label: Change breakfast
choices.result: Breakfast, and only breakfast, for now. It's a start, she says, and she means it kindly, and you notice the difference by Friday practice.

scenarios.title: The Sleep Study
scenarios.text: The club puts every rookie through a sleep study, and your results are embarrassing: five hours a night, phone in your hand until two, a bedtime that moves around like the wind.

choices.label: Fix your sleep
choices.result: Every recommendation: a dark room, no phone, the same bedtime. Your practices improve within two weeks, and you dream again.

choices.label: Just go to bed earlier
choices.result: An hour earlier, nothing fancier. It helps a lot, and your phone still comes to bed with you, which the sleep coach pretends not to know.

choices.label: Compare results at lunch
choices.result: Everyone's results are terrible, it turns out. You laugh about it for a week, and the rookies start a 'lights out by ten' bet for push-ups.

scenarios.title: The Team Psychologist
scenarios.text: The club's team psychologist stops you in the hallway and offers you a standing Tuesday appointment. No pressure, they say; most of the veterans have one.

choices.label: Take the Tuesday slot
choices.result: Tuesdays at two, every week. Some weeks you talk about kicking; most weeks you talk about everything else, and that's the point.

choices.label: Say you're fine
choices.result: Fine, you say, and you are, mostly. The psychologist leaves the door open with a small nod, and the Tuesday slot stays empty for weeks.

choices.label: Build a routine with them
choices.result: The sessions become a workshop for your pre-kick routine: breath, count, one thought. It's the best thing you do all year.

choices.label: Pick up where you left off
choices.result: What worked in college goes straight to the psychologist in the first session, so the two of you skip a month of getting to know each other.
choices.lock_text: having worked with a sports psychologist in college

scenarios.title: The Rookie Who Doesn't Make It
scenarios.text: The rookie you came in with is released after his first season. By noon his locker is empty, his nameplate is in the trash, and his parking spot already has someone else's car in it.

choices.label: Help him pack
choices.result: His things, carried to the car with you. He thanks you for being the only one who came, and you both pretend not to be upset.

choices.label: Kick harder
choices.result: Harder than you've kicked all year, that afternoon, alone on the far field. The empty locker is still there in the morning when you come in.

choices.label: Ask your agent what would have saved him
choices.result: What could have saved him? Your agent's answer is a list: the weight room, the meetings, the attitude. You take every item seriously.

scenarios.title: The Practice-Field Fan
scenarios.text: A kid watches every practice from behind the fence with a cardboard sign that has your name on it, spelled almost right. He's been there every day for two weeks.

choices.label: Go sign the sign
choices.result: Over to the fence after practice, and you sign the sign, fixing the spelling. He's there every day after that, beaming.

choices.label: Get him onto the field
choices.result: One kick on the real field, arranged with the club. He talks about it for years, and so do his parents.

choices.label: Wave every day
choices.result: A wave, every day, and you keep walking. He waves back every day with the whole sign, and by October the sign is spelled right.

scenarios.title: Kicks for the Hospital
scenarios.text: The club runs a kick-a-thon for the children's hospital, and you're the main event: a donation for every kick you make in an hour, with the patients watching from the sideline.

choices.label: Kick for the full hour
choices.result: A full hour without stopping. Your leg is jelly, and the total is the biggest the hospital has ever seen.

choices.label: Let the kids kick too
choices.result: Every kid gets a turn at the tee. The donations drop a little; the photos are the best of the year, and a nurse cries.

choices.label: Recruit the specialists
choices.result: The punter, the snapper and {holder} join in, and it turns into a contest. The crowd doubles, and so does the total.

scenarios.title: The Night Before Your Debut
scenarios.text: The night before your first regular-season game, and your phone won't stop: old coaches, cousins, a girl from your third-grade class. It's ten o'clock and you're wide awake.

choices.label: Phone off, early night
choices.result: The phone goes in a drawer at eight, and you read until you fall asleep. Nobody's message is more important than the morning.

choices.label: Answer two people
choices.result: {parent} and {best_friend}, nobody else. Their messages are the right ones, and you fall asleep with the phone on your chest.

choices.label: One more look at the plan
choices.result: The special teams plan, once more, then sleep. You walk in calm, and {coach} notices you're the only rookie not pacing.

scenarios.title: The Debut Week Interview
scenarios.text: The national broadcast crew wants five minutes with the rookie kicker before your first game. The producer has a clipboard and very specific ideas about your 'story'.

choices.label: Tell your real story
choices.result: Kicking in the backyard with {parent}, into a fence with a hole in it. It makes the broadcast, and {parent} watches it forty times.

choices.label: Keep it to football
choices.result: Football only, short and polite. The crew thanks you, nothing makes air, you're secretly glad, and {parent} is quietly disappointed for a day.

choices.label: Talk about the unit
choices.result: The snapper and {holder}, mostly, and how a kick is really three people. The specialists' chat is very happy, and {holder} pretends to be annoyed.

scenarios.title: The Team Photo
scenarios.text: The team photo, and you're in the back row next to a lineman who has never learned your name. He calls you 'kick' and asks which number you are.

choices.label: Introduce yourself again
choices.result: Your name, again, with a handshake. He laughs, and from then on he calls you by name, loudly, across the cafeteria.

choices.label: Smile for the flash
choices.result: A smile, the flash, and back to the locker room. You're the blurry one in the corner of the framed print.

choices.label: Organize a specialists' photo
choices.result: A specialists-only photo afterward, organized by you. It ends up framed in the facility hallway, and {holder} puts a copy on their fridge.

scenarios.title: The Rookie Payday Dinner
scenarios.text: Your rookie class decides to celebrate your first full paychecks together at a restaurant you can't pronounce, with a menu that doesn't have prices on it.

choices.label: Go and enjoy it
choices.result: The whole night, every course. The bill is absurd, the night is worth it, and you all take a photo with the chef.

choices.label: Suggest a cheaper place
choices.result: A cheaper place with the same view, you suggest. Half the class comes, the rest think you're cheap, and your half has more fun.

choices.label: Order in
choices.result: Takeout, alone, on the couch. Your account is happier than you are, and you see the photos the next morning.

scenarios.title: The Trainer's Warning
scenarios.text: A trainer stops you in the hallway and quietly warns you about the supplements a veteran keeps recommending to the rookies. Some of them, the trainer says, aren't on the approved list.

choices.label: Make a rule for yourself
choices.result: A rule, made that night: nothing the club hasn't approved, ever. You sleep better knowing it, and the trainer notices.

choices.label: Warn the other rookies
choices.result: The other rookies hear exactly what the trainer said, from you. Two of them throw theirs out that night, and one of them thanks you a year later.

choices.label: Let the veterans sort it out
choices.result: Not your business, you decide, and you never ask what the others are taking. You're fine. You're not sure all of them are.
